prompt: Basil wants to paint the slogan VIVAT KANGAROO on a wall. He wants different letters to be coloured differently, and the same letters to be coloured identically. How many colours will he need?

solutions.title: List the different letters
solutions.body:
Write each letter only the first time it appears:

V, I, A, T, K, N, G, R, O

That is **9** different letters, so 9 colours.

**Answer: (C) 9**

solutions.title: Count and subtract repeats
solutions.body:
VIVAT KANGAROO has $5 + 8 = 13$ letters. Repeats:

- V appears 2 times → 1 extra
- A appears 3 times → 2 extra
- O appears 2 times → 1 extra

$13 - 4 = 9$ colours.

**Answer: (C) 9**

prompt: A blackboard is 6 m wide. The width of the middle part is 3 m. The two other parts have equal width. How wide is the right-hand part?

In a plane, the rows are numbered from 1 to 25, but there is no row number 13. Row number 15 has only 4 passenger seats, all the rest have 6 passenger seats. How many seats for passengers are there in the plane?

solutions.title: Count the rows
solutions.body:
Rows 1 to 25 would be 25 rows, but row 13 is missing: **24 rows**.

- 23 rows have 6 seats: $23 \times 6 = 138$
- Row 15 has 4 seats

Total: $138 + 4 = 142$.

**Answer: (D) 142**

solutions.title: Start full, then subtract
solutions.body:
If all 24 rows had 6 seats: $24 \times 6 = 144$. Row 15 has 2 seats fewer: $144 - 2 = 142$.

(Careful: 150 would be 25 full rows — but there is no row 13!)

**Answer: (D) 142**

prompt: When it is 4 o'clock in the afternoon in London, it is 5 o'clock in the afternoon in Madrid and it is 8 o'clock in the morning on the same day in San Francisco. Ann went to bed in San Francisco at 9 o'clock yesterday evening. What was the time in Madrid at that moment?

solutions.title: Find the time difference
solutions.body:
When it is 8 a.m. in San Francisco it is 5 p.m. in Madrid. From 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. is **9 hours**, so Madrid is 9 hours ahead.

9 p.m. yesterday + 9 hours = 6 a.m. **this morning**.

**Answer: (E) 6 o'clock this morning**

solutions.title: Go through London
solutions.body:
- San Francisco is 8 hours behind London (8 a.m. vs 4 p.m.).
- Madrid is 1 hour ahead of London.

At 9 p.m. in San Francisco it is 5 a.m. in London, so it is 6 a.m. in Madrid — and since we passed midnight, that's this morning.

**Answer: (E)**

prompt: Vivien and Mike were given some apples and pears by their grandmother. They had 25 pieces of fruit in their basket altogether. On the way home Vivien ate 1 apple and 3 pears, and Mike ate 3 apples and 2 pears. At home they found out that they brought home the same number of pears as apples. How many pears were they given by their grandmother?

Three buses provide small tours of the city during the day. They all depart at 8 o’clock each morning from the rail station. The tours last 20 minutes, 30 minutes, and 24 minutes, respectively. When will it be the first time when the three bus drivers meet again at the railway station?

solutions.title: Least common multiple
solutions.body:
Each bus is back at the station at multiples of its tour time. We need the smallest number that is a multiple of 20, 30 and 24.

- Multiples of 30: 30, 60, 90, **120**, …
- 120 is a multiple of 20 ✓ and of 24 ✓ ($24 \times 5 = 120$).

120 minutes = 2 hours after 8:00, so **10:00 am**.

**Answer: (B) At 10:00 am**

prompt: The pattern in the picture is constructed from regular hexagons. Adam connects the centres of any two adjacent hexagons. Which of the following patterns is the result of Adam’s drawing?

An ant crawls along the edges of a cube, each of them 1 m long, starting from the leftmost bottom vertex. The ant wants to visit each of the other vertices at least once. It cannot crawl across the faces of the cube. What is the shortest distance it must crawl?

solutions.title: Count the vertices
solutions.body:
A cube has 8 vertices. The ant starts at one, so it must reach **7 new vertices**. Each edge takes it to at most one new vertex, so it needs at least 7 edges = 7 m.

Can it do it in exactly 7? Yes: go around the bottom square (3 edges: visits 3 new corners), go up (1 edge), then around the top square (3 edges). That's $3 + 1 + 3 = 7$ m, visiting all 8 vertices.

**Answer: (A) 7 m**

solutions.title: Why 6 m is too short
solutions.body:
With 6 edges the ant can reach at most 6 new vertices, but there are 7 others. So 6 m is impossible, and the bottom-square / up / top-square path shows 7 m works.

**Answer: (A) 7 m**

prompt: One balloon can lift a basket containing items weighing at most 80 kg. Two such balloons can lift the same basket containing items weighing at most 180 kg. What is the weight of the basket?

solutions.title: What does the second balloon add?
solutions.body:
Adding one balloon lets us carry $180 - 80 = 100$ kg more. So **one balloon lifts 100 kg in total**.

With one balloon that 100 kg is the basket plus 80 kg of items, so the basket weighs $100 - 80 = 20$ kg.

**Answer: (B) 20 kg**

solutions.title: Check the answer
solutions.body:
If the basket weighs 20 kg:

- one balloon lifts $20 + 80 = 100$ kg,
- two balloons lift $20 + 180 = 200$ kg $= 2 \times 100$ ✓

**Answer: (B) 20 kg**

choices.text: It depends on the speed of rotation

prompt: Which three pieces should be added to complete the puzzle?

Lisa has 8 dice with the letters A, B, C and D, the same letter on all sides of each die. She builds a block with them. Two adjacent dice always have different letters. What letter is on the die that cannot be seen in the picture (in the far bottom corner of the block)?

solutions.title: Look at the hidden die's neighbours
solutions.body:
The hidden die (back, bottom, left) touches three dice:

- the die **above** it (back, top, left): **C**
- the die **in front** of it (front, bottom, left): **A**
- the die **beside** it (back, bottom, right): **D** (seen on the right side)

It must be different from C, A and D, so it is **B**.

**Answer: (B) B**

solutions.title: Label all the dice
solutions.body:
Top layer: front-left B, front-right D, back-left C, back-right A.
Bottom layer: front-left A, front-right B, back-right D, back-left ?.

The letters A, C, D are all next to the hidden die, and E is not one of Lisa's letters. Only B remains — and B only touches the hidden die diagonally, which is allowed.

**Answer: (B) B**

prompt: The positive integers have been coloured red, blue or green: 1 is red, 2 is blue, 3 is green, 4 is red, 5 is blue, 6 is green, and so on. Renate calculates the sum of a red number and a blue number. What colour can the resulting number be?

solutions.title: Use remainders
solutions.body:
- Red numbers: 1, 4, 7, … leave remainder **1** when divided by 3.
- Blue numbers: 2, 5, 8, … leave remainder **2**.
- Green numbers: 3, 6, 9, … are multiples of 3.

Red + blue leaves remainder $1 + 2 = 3$, i.e. a multiple of 3 → **green**, always.

**Answer: (C) only green**

solutions.title: Try examples
solutions.body:
- $1 + 2 = 3$ green
- $4 + 5 = 9$ green
- $7 + 2 = 9$ green
- $10 + 11 = 21$ green

Every example is green — and the remainder idea explains why it always happens.

**Answer: (C) only green**

prompt: There are 4 gearwheels on fixed axles next to each other, as shown. The first one has 30 gears, the second one 15, the third one 60 and the last one 10. How many revolutions does the last gearwheel make, when the first one turns through one revolution?

solutions.title: Count teeth passing
solutions.body:
When wheels mesh, the same number of teeth pass the contact point on both wheels.

One turn of the first wheel moves **30 teeth**. That pushes 30 teeth of the second wheel, which pushes 30 teeth of the third, which pushes 30 teeth of the last wheel.

The last wheel has 10 teeth, so it turns $30 \div 10 = 3$ times.

**Answer: (A) 3**

solutions.title: Wheel by wheel
solutions.body:
- Wheel 1 (30) turns once → wheel 2 (15) turns $30 \div 15 = 2$ times.
- Wheel 2 turning 2 times = 30 teeth → wheel 3 (60) turns $\frac{30}{60} = \frac12$ a turn.
- Half a turn of wheel 3 = 30 teeth → wheel 4 (10) turns 3 times.

The middle wheels don't change the answer!

**Answer: (A) 3**

prompt: Fifteen numbers are arranged in a row so that the sum of any four consecutive numbers is 12. Three numbers are already given in their cells of the row (see the picture). What number must be in the cell marked by ☺?

solutions.title: The row repeats every 4 cells
solutions.body:
Compare cells 1–4 with cells 2–5: both add to 12, and they share cells 2, 3, 4. So **cell 5 = cell 1**. In the same way, every number equals the number 4 places before it.

Number the cells 1 to 15:

- 1 is in cell 1 → the "position 1" numbers are 1
- 4 is in cell 8 → same as cell 4
- ☺ is in cell 10 → same as cell 2
- 2 is in cell 15 → same as cell 3

Cells 1–4 hold 1, ☺, 2, 4 and add to 12: $1 + ☺ + 2 + 4 = 12$, so ☺ = **5**.

**Answer: (D) 5**

solutions.title: Fill in the pattern
solutions.body:
Using the repeat-every-4 rule, the row is

1, ☺, 2, 4, 1, ☺, 2, 4, 1, ☺, 2, 4, 1, ☺, 2

Check positions: cell 8 is 4 ✓, cell 15 is 2 ✓, and cell 10 is ☺ ✓.

Any four in a row: $1 + ☺ + 2 + 4 = 12$ → ☺ = 5.

**Answer: (D) 5**

prompt: Both figures on the right are formed from the same five pieces. One of the pieces is a rectangle with a length of 10 cm and a width of 5 cm, and the other pieces are quarters of two different circles. What is the difference in the perimeter lengths of the figures?

solutions.title: Find the radii, then compare straight edges
solutions.body:
In the right figure the bottom is: small quarter circle + rectangle (10 cm) + small quarter circle, and the rectangle is 5 cm tall, so the small radius is **5 cm**. The big quarter circles make a half circle across the whole width $5 + 10 + 5 = 20$ cm, so the big radius is **10 cm**.

Both figures use all four curved arcs on the outside, so the curved parts are equal. Only the **straight** parts on the outside differ:

- **Right figure:** only the bottom of the rectangle, 10 cm.
- **Left figure:** one straight side of each big quarter circle ($10 + 10$) and one straight side of each small quarter circle ($5 + 5$): 30 cm.

Difference: $30 - 10 = 20$ cm.

**Answer: (D) 20 cm**

solutions.title: Count hidden edges
solutions.body:
Total straight length of all pieces: rectangle $10+5+10+5 = 30$, big quarters $2 \times (10+10) = 40$, small quarters $2 \times (5+5) = 20$. Total 90 cm.

When two straight edges are glued together, both disappear from the perimeter.

- **Left figure:** glued lengths are 10 (top of rectangle) + 10 (bottom) + 5 + 5 (sides) = 30, so $90 - 2\times30 = 30$ cm of straight edge shows.
- **Right figure:** glued lengths: big quarters to each other 10, big quarters to the bottom row 20, rectangle sides to small quarters $5+5$ = 40, so $90 - 2\times40 = 10$ cm shows.

The arcs are the same in both, so the difference is $30 - 10 = 20$ cm.

**Answer: (D) 20 cm**

prompt: A regular octagon is folded in half exactly three times until a triangle is obtained, as shown. Then the vertex is cut off at right angles, as shown in the picture. If we unfold the paper, what will it look like?
You can choose any two triangles and overlap them as you want. Which of the following polygons cannot be the shape of the overlapping part?

choices.text: any of the polygons in (A), (B), (C), (D) can be obtained

solutions.title: Draw them
solutions.body:
- **Triangle:** put a small triangle completely inside a big one.
- **Quadrilateral:** slide one triangle so that one corner of it pokes into the other — the overlap has 4 sides.
- **Pentagon:** cut off two corners of one triangle with a side of the other.
- **Hexagon:** draw a "Star of David": two equal triangles, one upside down. The overlap is a hexagon.

All four shapes are possible.

**Answer: (E)**

solutions.title: Count the sides
solutions.body:
Each side of the overlap lies on a side of one of the two triangles. Two triangles have 6 sides in total, so the overlap can have **at most 6 sides**. By moving the triangles you can get any number of sides from 3 to 6 (see the drawings in the other method).

So none of the shapes A–D is impossible.

**Answer: (E)**

prompt: A rubber ball falls vertically from the roof of a house, at a height of 10 m. After each impact on the ground it bounces back up to $\frac{4}{5}$ of its previous height. How many times will the ball appear in front of a rectangular window whose bottom edge is at a height of 5 m and whose top edge is at a height of 6 m?

solutions.title: Track each bounce
solutions.body:
Bounce heights: $10 \to 8 \to 6.4 \to 5.12 \to 4.096 \to \dots$

- Falling from 10 m: passes the window **1** time.
- Up to 8 m and down: passes going up and coming down: **2** times.
- Up to 6.4 m and down: above the top of the window, so again **2** times.
- Up to 5.12 m: it rises into the window, turns around inside it, and drops out — **1** time.
- Up to 4.096 m: never reaches the window.

Total: $1 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 6$.

**Answer: (D) 6**

solutions.title: Compare heights with the window
solutions.body:
Each bounce height decides what happens:

| Highest point | Appearances |
|---|---|
| 10 m (start, falling only) | 1 |
| 8 m (above 6 m) | 2 |
| 6.4 m (above 6 m) | 2 |
| 5.12 m (between 5 and 6 m) | 1 |
| 4.096 m (below 5 m) | 0 |

$1 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 6$.

**Answer: (D) 6**

prompt: Kangaroos Hip and Hop play jumping by hopping over a stone, then landing across so that the stone is in the middle of the segment travelled during each jump. Picture 1 shows how Hop jumped three times hopping over stones marked 1, 2 and 3. Hip has the configuration of stones marked 1, 2 and 3 (to jump over in this order), but starts in a different place as shown in Picture 2. Which of the points A, B, C, D or E is his landing point?

solutions.title: Jump square by square
solutions.body:
Use Picture 2 and count grid squares from START (right = +, up = +).

- Stone 1 is 2 up from START. Jumping over it lands **2 more up**: (0, 4).
- Stone 2 is at (4, 5). From (0, 4) that is 4 right and 1 up, so Hip lands another 4 right, 1 up: **(8, 6)**.
- Stone 3 is at (6, 3). From (8, 6) that is 2 left and 3 down, so Hip lands another 2 left, 3 down: **(4, 0)**.

(4, 0) is 4 squares right of START on the same line — point **D**.

**Answer: (D) D**

solutions.title: Each jump doubles the step to the stone
solutions.body:
A jump over a stone moves Hip by **twice** the arrow from where he is to the stone.

- START → stone 1: (0, 2), doubled (0, 4). Hip at (0, 4).
- (0, 4) → stone 2 (4, 5): arrow (4, 1), doubled (8, 2). Hip at (8, 6).
- (8, 6) → stone 3 (6, 3): arrow (−2, −3), doubled (−4, −6). Hip at (4, 0).

That is point D.

**Answer: (D) D**

prompt: Winnie's vinegar-wine-water marinade contains vinegar and wine in the ratio 1 to 2, and wine and water in the ratio 3 to 1. Which of the following statements is true?

choices.text: There is more vinegar than wine.
There is more wine than vinegar and water together.
There is more vinegar than wine and water together.
There is more water than vinegar and wine together.
There is less vinegar than either water or wine.

solutions.title: Make the wine match
solutions.body:
Vinegar : wine = 1 : 2 = **3 : 6**. Wine : water = 3 : 1 = **6 : 2**.

So vinegar : wine : water = 3 : 6 : 2. Say 3 cups vinegar, 6 cups wine, 2 cups water.

- A: 3 > 6? ✗
- B: 6 > 3 + 2 = 5 ✓
- C: 3 > 8? ✗
- D: 2 > 9? ✗
- E: 3 < 2? ✗

**Answer: (B)**

solutions.title: Pick a nice amount of wine
solutions.body:
Choose 6 L of wine (it works with both ratios).

- Vinegar is half the wine: 3 L.
- Water is a third of the wine: 2 L.

Wine (6 L) is more than vinegar and water together (5 L).

**Answer: (B)**

prompt: Peter wants to cut a rectangle of size $6\times7$ into squares with side lengths that are whole numbers. What is the minimal number of squares he can get? (All parts must be squares.)

solutions.title: Find a cut with 5 squares
solutions.body:
- Cut a $4\times4$ square from one corner of the $6 \times 7$ (4 along the 6-side, 4 along the 7-side).
- Next to it along the 6-side, the leftover $2 \times 4$ strip makes **two $2\times2$** squares.
- The remaining $6 \times 3$ strip makes **two $3\times3$** squares.

That's $1 + 2 + 2 = 5$ squares: $16 + 4 + 4 + 9 + 9 = 42$ ✓.

**Answer: (B) 5**

solutions.title: Why 4 squares cannot work
solutions.body:
Four whole-number squares must have areas adding to $6 \times 7 = 42$. The only ways are

- $36 + 4 + 1 + 1$ (sides 6, 2, 1, 1): after the $6\times6$ a $6\times1$ strip is left, which needs six $1\times1$ squares ✗
- $25 + 9 + 4 + 4$ (5, 3, 2, 2): after the $5\times5$ the leftover strips are only 1 or 2 wide, so a $3\times3$ can't fit ✗
- $16 + 16 + 9 + 1$ (4, 4, 3, 1): two $4\times4$ squares need 8 cm side by side, but the rectangle is only 6 by 7 ✗

So 4 is impossible and 5 is the minimum.

**Answer: (B) 5**

prompt: Rectangle ABCD is cut into four smaller rectangles, as shown in the figure. The four smaller rectangles have the following properties: (a) the perimeters of three of them are 11, 16 and 19; (b) the perimeter of the fourth is neither the biggest nor the smallest of the four. What is the perimeter of the original rectangle ABCD?

solutions.title: Opposite rectangles
solutions.body:
Two diagonally opposite small rectangles together use every side length of the big rectangle once, so **their perimeters add up to the perimeter of ABCD**. That works for both diagonal pairs.

So the fourth perimeter $x$ plus its opposite equals the sum of the other two:

- opposite 11: $x = 16 + 19 - 11 = 24$ — the biggest ✗
- opposite 16: $x = 11 + 19 - 16 = 14$ — in the middle ✓
- opposite 19: $x = 11 + 16 - 19 = 8$ — the smallest ✗

So $x = 14$ is opposite 16, and the perimeter of ABCD is $16 + 14 = 11 + 19 = 30$.

**Answer: (A) 30**

solutions.title: Use letters for the pieces
solutions.body:
Let the big rectangle be split into widths $a, b$ and heights $c, d$. The four perimeters are $2(a+c)$, $2(b+c)$, $2(a+d)$, $2(b+d)$, and the big perimeter is $2(a+b+c+d)$.

Notice $2(a+c) + 2(b+d) = 2(b+c) + 2(a+d) =$ big perimeter. With the numbers 11, 16, 19 and an in-between fourth value, the only match is $11 + 19 = 16 + 14 = 30$.

**Answer: (A) 30**

prompt: Twelve numbers, from 1 to 12, are arranged in a circle so that any neighbouring numbers always differ by either 1 or 2. Which of the following pairs of numbers have to be neighbours?

solutions.title: Start from the smallest number
solutions.body:
- 1 can only sit next to 2 and 3, so its two neighbours are 2 and 3.
- 2 and 3 can't also be neighbours of each other (the circle would close with only 3 numbers). So 2's other neighbour is 4, and 3's other neighbour is 5.
- Likewise 4 → 6, 5 → 7, 6 → 8, 7 → 9, 8 → 10, 9 → 11, 10 → 12, and 11 – 12 closes the circle.

The circle is 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 11, 9, 7, 5, 3. **8 and 10** are neighbours.

**Answer: (C) 8 and 10**

solutions.title: Evens on one side, odds on the other
solutions.body:
Going around, the circle climbs up through the even numbers 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 and comes back down through the odd numbers 11, 9, 7, 5, 3, 1. (You can check that any other arrangement gets stuck.)

So consecutive numbers like 5 & 6 or 3 & 4 are **not** next to each other (except 1 & 2 and 11 & 12), while numbers 2 apart of the same parity are — such as 8 and 10.

**Answer: (C) 8 and 10**

prompt: Several cells of a $4\times4$ table were coloured grey. The number of grey cells in each row was indicated to the right of it. The number of grey cells in each column was indicated at the bottom of it. Then the grey colour was washed off. Which of the following tables can be the result?

Adam's house number has three digits. Removing the leftmost digit of this number, you obtain the house number of Adam's friend Ben. Removing the leftmost digit of Ben's house number, you obtain the house number of Chiara. The sum of the three house numbers is 912. What is the middle (the tens) digit of Adam's house number?

solutions.title: Look at the ones digit first
solutions.body:
Write Adam's number as $\overline{abc}$. Then Ben's is $\overline{bc}$ and Chiara's is $c$.

- Ones column: $c + c + c = 3c$ must end in 2, so $c = 4$ ($3 \times 4 = 12$, carry 1).
- Tens column: $b + b + 1 = 2b + 1$ must end in 1, so $b = 0$ or $b = 5$.
  - $b = 0$ would make Ben's number "04", which isn't a two-digit house number.
  - $b = 5$: $2 \times 5 + 1 = 11$, carry 1.
- Hundreds column: $a + 1 = 9$, so $a = 8$.

Check: $854 + 54 + 4 = 912$ ✓. The tens digit is **5**.

**Answer: (A) 5**

solutions.title: Count how often each digit appears
solutions.body:
The hundreds digit appears once (worth $100a$), the tens digit twice ($20b$), the ones digit three times ($3c$):

$100a + 20b + 3c = 912$.

$3c$ must end in 2 → $c = 4$, leaving $100a + 20b = 900$, i.e. $5a + b = 45$. With $b$ a nonzero digit (so Ben's number really has two digits), $a = 8, b = 5$.

**Answer: (A) 5**

prompt: There are seven cities in Wonderland. Each pair of cities is connected by one road, either visible or invisible. On the map of Wonderland, there are only twelve visible roads, as shown. Alice has magical glasses: when she looks at the map through these glasses she only sees the roads that are otherwise invisible. How many invisible roads can she see?

solutions.title: Count all roads
solutions.body:
Each city connects to the 6 other cities: $7 \times 6 = 42$, but this counts every road twice (once from each end), so there are $42 \div 2 = 21$ roads.

Invisible roads: $21 - 12 = 9$.

**Answer: (D) 9**

solutions.title: Add up city by city
solutions.body:
Number the cities 1 to 7. Count roads to cities with bigger numbers only:

$6 + 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 0 = 21$ roads in total.

12 are visible, so $21 - 12 = 9$ are invisible.

**Answer: (D) 9**

prompt:
Ann and Bill participate in a math reality show. Each of them is secretly given one positive integer. They know that their numbers are two consecutive numbers (for instance, Ann's number is 7, Bill's number is 6). They know only their own number, and they have to guess the number of the other person. Ann and Bill have the following discussion:

- Ann to Bill: "I do not know your number."
- Bill to Ann: "I do not know your number."
- Ann to Bill: "Now I know your number! It is a factor of 20."

What is Ann's number?

solutions.title: Follow what each statement tells us
solutions.body:
1. **Ann doesn't know.** If Ann had 1, Bill would have to be 2. So Ann's number is **not 1**.
2. **Bill doesn't know.** If Bill had 1, he'd know Ann has 2. If Bill had 2, Ann would be 1 or 3 — but Ann isn't 1, so he'd know it's 3. So Bill's number is **not 1 or 2**.
3. **Now Ann knows.** Ann's choices for Bill are her number minus 1 or plus 1. She can rule one out only if it's 1 or 2. So Ann has 2 (Bill is 3) or 3 (Bill is 4).

Bill's number is a factor of 20: 4 is, 3 isn't. So Bill has 4 and **Ann has 3**.

**Answer: (C) 3**

solutions.title: Test the choices
solutions.body:
- Ann = 1: she'd know at once that Bill has 2 ✗
- Ann = 2: after the talk she'd know Bill has 3 — not a factor of 20 ✗
- Ann = 3: Bill is 2 or 4; Bill said he didn't know, so he isn't 2 (with 2 he'd have known Ann is 3). Bill = 4, a factor of 20 ✓
- Ann = 4 or 5: Bill could be 3 or 5 (or 4 or 6) — Ann still couldn't tell ✗

**Answer: (C) 3**

prompt: A square-shaped piece of paper is folded twice as shown in the picture. The area of the original square is 64 cm². What is the total area of the shaded rectangles?

A craftsman is asked to manufacture three universal weights so that, using only these weights and a simple balancing scale, it will be possible to measure any mass of consecutive whole numbers of grams, starting from 1 gram, 2 grams, etc., up to a maximum possible mass of N grams. It is allowed to place any of the three weights on either side of the balancing scale, or to put any of them aside. What is the greatest possible mass, N grams, that one can measure, given these requirements?

solutions.title: Weights 1 g, 3 g and 9 g
solutions.body:
Use weights of **1, 3 and 9 g**. A weight on the same side as the object counts as *minus*. Then:

1, 2 = 3−1, 3, 4 = 3+1, 5 = 9−3−1, 6 = 9−3, 7 = 9+1−3, 8 = 9−1, 9, 10 = 9+1, 11 = 9+3−1, 12 = 9+3, 13 = 9+3+1.

Every mass from 1 to 13 g works.

**Answer: (E) 13 g**

solutions.title: Why not more than 13
solutions.body:
Each weight has 3 choices: left pan, right pan, or aside. That gives $3 \times 3 \times 3 = 27$ arrangements. One of them is "all aside" (0 g), and the rest come in mirror pairs (swap the pans) that measure the same mass. So at most $(27 - 1) \div 2 = 13$ different masses can be measured. The 1-3-9 set reaches exactly 13.

**Answer: (E) 13 g**
